topic: OkHttp internals: interceptor chain, connections & HTTP/2

questions.question: You want to log every call exactly once, including calls answered from OkHttp's cache and calls that were redirected. Which kind of interceptor should you add?
options: An application interceptor with `addInterceptor()`
A network interceptor with `addNetworkInterceptor()`
An `Authenticator`
An `EventListener` registered per connection
questions.explanation: Application interceptors sit at the top of the chain and run once per call, regardless of redirects, retries or cache hits. Network interceptors run once per actual network request, so they are skipped for cache hits and run again for each redirect.

questions.question: Creating a new `OkHttpClient` for every request is fine, because all clients share one global connection pool.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each client built from scratch gets its own connection pool and dispatcher, so separate clients cannot reuse each other's connections and waste threads and memory. Share one client and use `newBuilder()` when you need a variant; derived clients share the pool.

questions.question: What happens if code reads `response.code` but never closes the response body?
options: Nothing, because the body is closed when the Response is garbage-collected
OkHttp throws an exception on the next request
The response is automatically written to the cache
The connection cannot go back to the pool, so it leaks and later requests may need new connections
questions.explanation: A connection is only released for reuse once its response body has been fully read or closed. Unclosed bodies leak connections, and OkHttp logs a warning about a leaked connection when it notices. Use `use {}` or read the body fully.

questions.question: In what order does a request pass through OkHttp's interceptor chain?
options: Retry/redirect, your application interceptors, cache, your network interceptors, connect, then the server call
Your application interceptors, retry/redirect, bridge, cache, connect, your network interceptors, then the server call
Your network interceptors, cache, connect, your application interceptors, then the server call
Cache, your application interceptors, connect, retry/redirect, then the server call
questions.explanation: Application interceptors wrap everything, then OkHttp's retry/follow-up, the bridge that adds headers like gzip, the cache and the connection step run. Network interceptors come after a connection exists, right before the request is written to the server. That is why only network interceptors see the connection and OkHttp's added headers.

questions.question: You `enqueue()` 100 calls to one HTTP/2 host at once. What limits how many are in flight concurrently by default?
options: The connection pool's maximum idle connections
The number of CPU cores on the device
The Dispatcher's per-host limit on running async calls, which is small by default
The HTTP/2 server's stream limit, and nothing on the client
questions.explanation: The Dispatcher caps running async calls in total and per host (64 and 5 by default); the rest wait in a queue. With HTTP/2 those running calls are multiplexed on one connection, but the Dispatcher limit still applies. Idle-pool settings only control how many unused connections are kept.

questions.question: What can a network interceptor do or see that an application interceptor cannot? Select all that apply.
options: Run for responses served entirely from OkHttp's cache
Access the `Connection` the request will be sent on
Return a made-up response without calling `proceed()`
Observe each hop of a redirect as a separate request
See headers OkHttp adds itself, such as `Accept-Encoding: gzip`
questions.explanation: Network interceptors run after the bridge and connect steps, once per real network request, so they see the connection, OkHttp's headers and each redirect. They do not run for cache hits because no network request happens, and they must call `proceed()` exactly once, so short-circuiting is an application interceptor's job.

questions.question: If you add an `Accept-Encoding: gzip` header to requests yourself, OkHttp stops transparently decompressing the response body for you.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: OkHttp only decompresses transparently when it added the header itself. If you set it, OkHttp assumes you want to handle the encoding and hands you the compressed bytes, which often shows up as garbage JSON parse errors.

questions.question: You refresh tokens in an OkHttp `Authenticator`. When the token expires, ten parallel requests all get 401 and the backend sees ten refresh calls, some of which invalidate each other. What is the best fix?
options: Synchronize refresh, and before refreshing, check whether the failed request's token is older than the current one; if so, just retry with the current token
Return `null` from the Authenticator so OkHttp retries automatically
Lower the Dispatcher's per-host limit to one
Move the refresh into a network interceptor so it runs once per connection
questions.explanation: Each 401 triggers the Authenticator independently, so refresh must be serialized, and late arrivals should reuse the token someone else already refreshed. Returning `null` gives up and delivers the 401; a network interceptor does not reduce parallelism; limiting the Dispatcher to one would throttle the whole app.

questions.question: Which statements about OkHttp's HTTP cache are true? Select all that apply.
options: Nothing is cached unless the client is built with a `Cache` pointing at a directory
A request with `CacheControl.FORCE_CACHE` that misses the cache gets a 504 response instead of going to the network
An application interceptor that rewrites a response's `Cache-Control` header changes what gets stored
A network interceptor that rewrites a response's `Cache-Control` header changes what gets stored
POST responses are cached by default
questions.explanation: The cache is opt-in, and forcing cache on a miss produces a synthetic 504. The cache step sits between application and network interceptors, so a network interceptor's header changes are seen before storage, while an application interceptor only sees the response after it was cached. Only GET responses are cached.

questions.question: A server sends one byte every 5 seconds. The client has `readTimeout = 10s` and no `callTimeout`. What happens when downloading a 1 MB response?
options: The call fails after the default call timeout
The call fails after 10 seconds with a read timeout
The read timeout never fires because it applies to each read, so the download can take days
OkHttp detects the slow server and switches to HTTP/2
questions.explanation: Read timeout is the maximum gap between bytes, and data keeps arriving within it, so it never triggers. `callTimeout` bounds the entire call, from DNS to the end of the body, and is disabled by default. Set it when you need a hard limit on total time.
